newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ramos promises not to be a lame-duck.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos promises not to be a lame-duck.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos, forced to take a helicopter to avoid thousands of protesters, on Monday pledged to press on with his reforms in a speech his office called his swansong to the nation.

Hundreds of police in riot gear blocked the path of more than 10,000 mostly leftist workers who were marching to Congress where Ramos was speaking. They were protesting that the president's reforms were destroying the country and lining the pockets of foreigners.

The crush of demonstrators blocked the main road leading away for the legislature, forcing the motorcade of popular vice-president Joseph Estrada to turn back while Ramos was flown out by helicopter after his speech.
"I will not be a lame duck president...because that is not my nature and because the times call for vigorous tigers and not enfeebled fowls," he told an enthusiastic Congress.

In his last state-of-the-nation address, Ramos patted himself on the back for turning around the long-ailing Philippine economy which is, after years of mismanagement, finally ready to join the other booming Asian tiger economies.
"We have laboured hard and unceasingly to restore our nation to stability, growth, equity and optimism, and for this the present and future generations will be grateful," he said.

On his way to the podium, he briefly shook hands with Imelda Marcos, now a congresswoman and widow of late dictator Ferdinand Marcos, the man many blame for bringing the country to its knees before he fled in 1986 after 20 years in power.
Ramos, whose six-year term finishes next June, reeled off economic statistics to prove that life for the mostly impoverished Filipinos had improved in the past five years under his rule.
But the next 10 to 15 years will pose the greatest challenges and the Philippines must match the economic growth of its neighbours if it is to be a serious player in the Asia-Pacific region.
"We must not allow growth to slow down, because only sustained development will enable us to wipe out Filipino poverty," Ramos said.
One of the region's few politically open societies, Ramos said democracy in the Philippines must not be allowed to falter.
"Freedom, markets and progress go together," he said.
The latest setback for the Philippines in the form of speculative pressure on its currency -- may turn out to be a help.
"The recent speculative attack on the peso may have been a blessing in disguise, because it gave us the opportunity to enhance the competitiveness of the peso," he said.
The peso has fallen about eight percent since the government was forced this month to allow an effective devaluation of the peso as speculators took on several central banks in the region.
"We paid a small price for the long-term stability and resilience of our economy," Ramos said.
But demonstrators accused the Ramos administration of doing little to spread wealth in a country where a third of the population lives below the poverty line.
Foreigners were allowed to exploit cheap labour and snap up land to turn into golf courses and holiday resorts, they said.
Protesters carried placards with slogans such as "Enough, enough. Let's end the Ramos regime", "Fight against imperialist globalisation" and "Enough of grinding poverty".

"The general (Ramos) is supposed to be singing his swansong today...but we have not counted him out. Like the cheat that he has always been, he has some aces up his sleeve," the leftist Nationalist Patriotic Alliance (Bayan) said in a statement.
"If he still fails, he may just have to do what his cousin Ferdinand Marcos did in 1972," it said, referring to Marcos's declaration of martial law.
As head of the police force, Ramos was instrumental in the downfall of Marcos who fled from the country in 1986 after the "people's power" revolution brought Corazon Aquino to the presidency.
